title: Firouzja Wins Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot
summary:
GM Alireza Firouzja came back from behind to win the Total Chess World Championship on its 10th and final day. He came into Friday down a set against GM Anish Giri, but won the second set 13-8. He went on to win the tournament and $80,000 in the armageddon tiebreaker.

Firouzja, Giri, GM Fabiano Caruana (third place), and GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave (fourth place) qualify for the 2027 tour.

The trophies. Photo: Tor Nilssen/Total Chess.

Knockout 1: Firouzja Wins Tournament, Caruana In 3rd

Knockout 2: Niemann Comes 5th, Beats Duda

Knockout 3: Martirosyan 9th Over Arjun

Knockout 4: Wesley So 13th Over Aronian

Knockout 5: Carlsen Forfeits Fast Classic, Wins Armageddon For 17th

Knockout 6: Praggnanandhaa 21st

The final day saw the second set of each match, with seven games played (or an eighth in case of an armageddon tiebreaker). The first three places qualify for next year's tour, but because Caruana and Giri already qualified through the 2026 FIDE Candidates Tournament, Vachier-Lagrave got one of those spots.

Prize Breakdown

Place | Player | Prize

1st | Alireza Firouzja | $80,000

2nd | Anish Giri | $50,000

3rd | Fabiano Caruana | $45,000

4th | Maxime Vachier-Lagrave | $40,000

5th | Hans Moke Niemann | $38,000

6th | Jan-Krzysztof Duda | $36,000

7th | Ian Nepomniachtchi | $34,000

8th | Liem Le | $32,000

9th | Haik M. Martirosyan | $30,000

10th | Arjun Erigaisi | $28,000

11th | Richard Rapport | $26,000

12th | Jorden van Foreest | $24,000

13th | Wesley So | $22,000

14th | Levon Aronian | $20,000

15th | Vincent Keymer | $19,000

16th | Shakhriyar Mamedyarov | $18,000

17th | Magnus Carlsen | $17,000

18th | Vladislav Artemiev | $16,000

19th | Andrew Hong | $15,000

20th | Bibisara Assaubayeva | $14,000

21st | Praggnanandhaa R | $13,000

22nd | Abhimanyu Mishra | $12,000

23rd | Nodirbek Abdusattorov | $11,000

24th | Vaishali Rameshbabu | $10,000

Keep reading, but you may also want to check out GM Hikaru Nakamura's recap video below.

Knockout 1: Firouzja Wins Tournament, Caruana In 3rd

Giri was flying high on Wednesday and Thursday, after beating Vachier-Lagrave in the Semifinals and winning set one against Firouzja in the Final. He joked that he played unusually well on those days, but "today I played the usual [level] somehow."

He did play 48 games of chess in the last 10 days, and he said the finale was a "combination of bad luck and some tiredness." Hinting at GM Magnus Carlsen (more on that later), he added, tongue-in-cheek, "I think in this tournament it's an achievement to show up... apparently it is an option not to show up!"

I think in this tournament it's an achievement to show up.

—Anish Giri

It was a close match that went to the tiebreaker, and Firouzja said, "I think we both deserved to win the match." He was understandably more positive about the format than anyone else, and the only thing he'd change is increasing the value of the blitz games. He said, "This format helps me more than anyone probably. I was very confident... but it's always tough."

This format helps me more than anyone probably. I was very confident... but it's always tough.

—Alireza Firouzja

Giri and Firouzja showed up. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

Giri won the first blitz game, but Firouzja turned the tide by winning the next two in a row, taking the lead for the first time in the match. In game three, Giri was so close to making a draw in the rook endgame but had just five seconds. 45...Rf2?? was the losing move.

Blitz game four was a cold shower, though, as he hung his bishop and Giri equalized the match 2-2.

After a break, Firouzja returned and won the first game of rapid chess with the black pieces to take a four-point lead. It was a King's Indian Defense where Giri gained the advantage with White but didn't hold onto it. Deep in the endgame, Firouzja drummed up a mating attack long after the queens were gone.

GM Dejan Bojkov analyzes the Game of the Day below. (His annotations will be added soon.)

With the white pieces in the next rapid game, Firouzja made a comfortable draw in the Alapin Sicilian—if anything, he was the only one with an advantage at various points. Then, he was rock-solid to draw the fast classic game to win the second set, reaching armageddon tiebreaks.

Giri had 10 minutes with the white pieces and Firouzja had seven minutes with Black plus draw odds. As Giri put it: "In the armageddon, I didn't even make it exciting... I was hoping the last game would be more spectacular." Giri got an isolated pawn position, and sacrificed it for some initiative. It didn't pan out, and Firouzja accepted a draw in a winning position on move 35.

Asked for his favorite moment of the event, Firouzja quipped: "The last moment!"

Norway Chess CEO Kjell Madland presents Firouzja the trophy. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

Even with the runner-up finish, Giri was proud of his performance and said, "I have confidence from this event... and I'm really happy it happened, and it went quite well, of course." This event gives him quite a confidence boost for the 2026 FIDE World Rapid & Blitz Championships, held in Istanbul at the end of December.

Moving on to the third-place match, Caruana said he was "actually not too tired" on the last day of play, and he won both sets against Vachier-Lagrave. "The last match ended quite well and it was also an early day," said Caruana, as theirs was one of the first matches to end.

Vachier-Lagrave vs. Caruana in the match for third. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

Caruana won the second set by just one point, and the first rapid game made the difference. Caruana said, "In blitz, he was definitely playing better than me, but in rapid he didn't play his best for sure. And I won that first game with white, and then it was a very difficult situation for him."

In blitz, he was definitely playing better than me, but in rapid he didn't play his best for sure.

—Fabiano Caruana

Vachier-Lagrave went winless for 21 games before this match, but he won the first three blitz games with just one draw in the fourth. In the first rapid game, however, Caruana won when he was allowed to create a runaway passed f-pawn. One mistake is all it takes! With two draws after that, the American won the match.

Speaking about the format, Caruana felt that the time control of 45+30 felt closer to a classical game than a rapid game. "The main thing, I think, is not to rush. Because it feels like you're kind of maybe playing rapid and you should, I think, get that feeling out of your mind and approach it like a classical game," he said.

As for his favorite moment of the event, it was beating GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu 2-0 in classically rated games on the third day.

Vachier-Lagrave finished fourth, but it's still enough for entry into the tour next year. He thought it was a difficult tournament, especially for those who played all the games. He said:

I'm a bit relieved that it's over. This was very tough and I didn't have the luxury to skip games... Overall, I think it was a very good experience. Maybe a bit too difficult, but at the same time once we all signed up for this, it was worth testing it out, and I'm a bit sad that some of the players decided to make their own headlines."

He later amended his statement to use stronger wording:

Correction: that a crybaby decided to make his own headlines.

— MVL (@Vachier_Lagrave) November 20, 2026

Knockout 2: Niemann Comes 5th

GM Hans Niemann dominated GM Jan-Krzysztof Duda on the first day, but the Polish number-one won the second set 11-10 on Friday to even the score. That led to an armageddon tiebreaker, which Niemann won with the black pieces. Seeing no winning chances with a pawn-down endgame, Duda resigned, as a draw and a loss led to the same match result.

Niemann said he had felt sick but was "happy I still have the clutch flagging skills." He looked forward to next year's event, although "I haven't been invited yet, but maybe this performance will result in a wildcard."

Hans Niemann after beating Jan-Krzysztof Duda to finish 5th: "I don't feel good at all today, but I'm happy I still have the clutch flagging skills! I mean, I had a good position as well." "I'm looking forward to next year. I mean, I haven't been invited yet." #TotalChess https://t.co/xpie2lcqfG

— Chess.com News (@ChesscomNews) November 20, 2026

As for the match for seventh and eighth, GM Ian Nepomniachtchi lost the second set but won in style with a King's Gambit in the armageddon game against GM Liem Le.

It was a fortunate bounceback for Nepomniachtchi, who led the second set before the fast classic game. There, he made a blunder on move nine and was lost after Le's 11.0-0!.

Knockout 3: Martirosyan 9th Over Arjun

So much happened at this tournament that it's easy to overlook GM Haik Martirosyan's two classically rated wins against super-GM Arjun Erigaisi, along the way to winning both sets in the match for ninth. That win was critical in the second set, as Arjun had been leading 9-3. Fatigue was clearly a factor as Arjun, who, after fighting his way to a pawn-down rook endgame, fell apart with eight minutes on the clock.

GM Richard Rapport beat GM Jorden van Foreest in the armageddon game to take 11th place.

Knockout 4: Wesley So 13th Over Aronian

GM Wesley So won the first set of the all-American matchup on Thursday, but GM Levon Aronian won the second set 11-10. In the end, So managed to draw the armageddon tiebreaker to win the match.

GM Vincent Keymer won the longest match of the day against GM Shakhriyar Mamedyarov after successfully holding a 90-move queen endgame to a draw in the fast classic encounter. The Azeri grandmaster found time during that endgame to sing happy birthday to his son from the confessional booth, the most wholesome clip of the day.

Shakhriyar Mamedyarov sings happy birthday to his son from the confessional booth! #TotalChess https://t.co/8ECv3XeB2Y

— Chess.com News (@ChesscomNews) November 20, 2026

Knockout 5: Carlsen Forfeits Fast Classic, Wins Armageddon For 17th

Carlsen won the match for 17th place against GM Vladislav Artemiev. Carlsen started with a one-point lead after winning blitz game two and drawing the others. He told Norwegian TV 2 that he achieved his goals of playing the Budapest Opening in Budapest and then playing the Fried Liver Attack as an homage to his wife—the only opening she knew when they met each other. The latter game was the one he won.

You can read the longer interview transcript, translated from Norwegian, but Carlsen said he didn't want to be at the tournament. He said:

At the bottom of things, it was tough for me to spend two weeks here right now with wanting to be with my family. And that has become very clear, that I'd rather be home than be here. And then that has become a negative spiral for me.

Things turned in Artemiev's favor in the rapid portion. In the first rapid game, Artemiev won a queen for rook and bishop but didn't win the game. But he did score the four points in the second rapid game to take the lead.

Carlsen did not arrive for the fast classic game and forfeited his fifth game in the tournament. A draw would have left him with a rating of 2801.8, but a loss would have sent him under 2800.

Carlsen never replied to 1.d4.

With an equal score at 1-1, Carlsen then returned and won the armageddon game with Black, taking advantage of Artemiev's time trouble in an equal rook endgame when the draw was already in hand.

Asked to explain his forfeited games, Carlsen told Total Chess: "The tournament is kind of over and, yeah, I wanted to play the games I wanted to play."

I wanted to play the games I wanted to play.

—Magnus Carlsen

GM Andrew Hong defeated GM Bibisara Assaubayeva in both sets to finish 19th.

Knockout 6: Praggnanandhaa 21st

GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu won both sets against GM Abhimanyu Mishra to finish 21st. GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov defeated GM Vaishali Rameshbabu 20-0 in the second set to finish 23r

additionalSources.title: Alireza Firouzja wins Total Chess Budapest Pilot
additionalSources.summary: Giri finishes second after Armageddon draw as Caruana secures third place Alireza Firouzja won the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot in Budapest on Friday after drawing the Armageddon decider with Black against Anish Giri. Firouzja had forced the tiebreak by winning the second day 12–8, after Giri took Thursday’s opening day 11–9. Fabiano Caruana secured third place with a second daily victory over Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, while five placement matches were decided by Armageddon. Each knockout day has seven games: four Blitz games, two Rapid games and one Fast Classic. A Blitz win is worth one point, a Rapid win four and a Fast Classic win eight, with half for a draw. The scores reset between days. Winning both days, or winning one and drawing the other, decides the match. One win apiece, or two drawn days, leads to Armageddon. Firouzja turns the final around All four blitz games in the final were decisive. Giri won the opener with White, Firouzja answered with two successive victories, and Giri won the fourth with Black to leave them level at 2–2. Firouzja then won the first rapid game with Black. A draw in the second gave him an 8–4 lead going into Fast Classic. Giri needed a Fast Classic victory to secure the title without a tiebreak, but the game was drawn. The four points apiece gave Firouzja a 12–8 daily victory and sent the final to Armageddon, with Giri playing White and Firouzja Black. The Armageddon game was drawn after 35 moves. With Black’s draw odds, Firouzja secured the Budapest pilot title, leaving Giri in second place. Caruana secures third place Vachier-Lagrave won the first three blitz games and drew the fourth to take a 3.5–0.5 lead. Caruana responded by winning the first rapid game with White, and a draw in the second put him ahead 6.5–5.5. Their Fast Classic game was drawn after 30 moves, completing a 10.5–9.5 daily victory for Caruana. Having also won Thursday 11–9, he secured third place without an Armageddon tiebreak, with Vachier-Lagrave finishing fourth. Rapport and Carlsen win Armageddon deciders Richard Rapport finished 11th after beating Jorden van Foreest with White in Armageddon. Van Foreest had leveled their match by winning Friday 12–8: the blitz games were split 2–2, he took a win and a draw in rapid, and Fast Classic was drawn. Rapport then won the decider in 32 moves, leaving Van Foreest in 12th place. Magnus Carlsen won his Armageddon game with Black against Vladislav Artemiev to secure 17th place. Carlsen edged Friday’s blitz 2.5–1.5, but Artemiev scored a win and a draw in rapid. The Fast Classic game was forfeited by Carlsen, giving Artemiev a 15.5–4.5 daily victory and forcing the Armageddon tiebreak. Carlsen’s win in the decider left Artemiev in 18th place. Three more matches settled in Armageddon Hans Moke Niemann finished fifth after beating Jan-Krzysztof Duda with Black in Armageddon. Duda had forced the tiebreak with an 11–9 daily victory, taking the blitz 3–1 before the players exchanged rapid wins and drew Fast Classic. Niemann’s win in the decider left Duda in sixth place. Ian Nepomniachtchi won his Armageddon game with White against Le Quang Liem to finish seventh. Le had won Fast Classic with White to take the day 14–6, reversing Thursday’s score after both the blitz and rapid portions were shared equally. Nepomniachtchi’s tiebreak victory left Le in eighth place. Wesley So secured 13th place by drawing the Armageddon game with Black against Levon Aronian. Black’s draw odds gave So the match, with Aronian finishing 14th. Aronian had won Friday 11–9 after taking three of the four blitz games, exchanging rapid wins and drawing Fast Classic. Placement matches completed Haik Martirosyan won Fast Classic with White against Arjun Erigaisi to turn a 3–9 deficit into an 11–9 daily victory and secure ninth place. Erigaisi had won the blitz 3–1 and taken a win and a draw in rapid, but Martirosyan’s victory gave him a second daily win after Thursday’s 14.5–5.5 result. Erigaisi finished tenth. Vincent Keymer secured 15th place after drawing his Fast Classic game with Shakhriyar Mamedyarov. The players had been level at 6–6 after blitz and rapid, and the four points apiece from the Fast Classic draw made Friday’s score 10–10. Keymer’s 14.5–5.5 victory on Thursday therefore settled the match, with Mamedyarov finishing 16th. Andrew Hong finished 19th after drawing Fast Classic against Bibisara Assaubayeva to take Friday’s play 13–7. He had won the blitz 3–1 and taken a win and a draw in rapid. Hong’s second daily victory, following Thursday’s 15–5 win, left Assaubayeva in 20th place. Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu won Fast Classic with Black against Abhimanyu Mishra to complete a 15–5 daily victory and secure 21st place. Praggnanandhaa took the blitz 3–1 and drew both rapid games before winning the final game in 38 moves. Having also won Thursday 12–8, he settled the match without a tiebreak, leaving Mishra in 22nd place. Nodirbek Abdusattorov won all seven games for a 20–0 daily victory against Vaishali Rameshbabu. His Fast Classic win with White completed a second successful day following Thursday’s 16–4 result. Abdusattorov finished 23rd and Vaishali 24th. title: Lazavik Cruises Into Speed Chess Quarterfinals With 12-8 Win Over Andreikin
summary:
GM Denis Lazavik is through to face either GM Wesley So or GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu in the Quarterfinals of the Speed Chess Championship XI after defeating GM Dmitry Andreikin 12-8 in the Round of 16. Lazavik won the first game before drawing the rest of the five-minute games as Andreikin became more and more frustrated at missed wins. Andreikin's first win only came in the 16th game of the match, when he'd already been blown away in 3+1. Lazavik earned $6,500 and Andreikin $1,625 by win percentage.

The next Round of 16 match, between GMs Alireza Firouzja and Vladislav Artemiev, will be on Friday, November 27 at 12:30 p.m. ET / 18:30 CET / 11 p.m. IST.

5+1: Lazavik 4-3 Andreikin

3+1: Lazavik 5.5-1.5 Andreikin

1+1: Lazavik 2.5-3.5 Andreikin

Lazavik joins GM Hikaru Nakamura in the Quarterfinals.

2026 Speed Chess Championship Bracket

Andreikin and Lazavik went into the match occupying the third and fourth spots on the Champions Chess Tour leaderboard, which will determine 12 players who qualify for the 2027 Esports World Cup.

Champions Chess Tour Leaderboard

See full leaderboard

The Speed Chess Championship is one of three events that count toward the CCT leaderboard. The other two paths to qualification are the Titled Tuesday Grand Prix and next year's Chess.com Open. Last year's EWC champion, GM Magnus Carlsen, gets an automatic entry.

Lazavik 12-8 Andreikin

The players went into the match with their stats very closely matched—except for the 16-year age gap.

Andreikin is a player with a 2743 peak rating, who in 2013 finished runner-up in the World Cup.

Lazavik, who competes for the esports team All Gamers, has enormous pedigree in fast chess. He finished third in the Speed Chess Championship earlier this year in London, then took the runner-up spot and $190,000 in the Esports World Cup in Paris. His over-the-board results haven't been quite as stellar so far, but he's recently climbed from <2600 to 2650 on the classical rating list after winning a string of individual events.

He commented in an interview before the Speed Chess Championship:

This year I played three classical tournaments and I performed in every tournament really well, I showed 2750 performance, something like this, and I’m very happy that I not only can play online in rapid and blitz but I can also play classical chess.

Our stats team made Lazavik the clear pre-match favorite, and did predict 3+1 as his best segment, though not the margin of his dominance there or that Andreikin would win the 1+1.

In the match, Lazavik was initially coming under heavy pressure in the 5+1 section. He confessed:

He constantly outplayed me, but then somehow maybe he just got tired and he just started blundering, and also when we got time scrambles he did not play well. He also started tilting a bit.

He also started tilting a bit.

—Lazavik on Andreikin

The final scores looked as follows:

5+1: Lazavik 4-3 Andreikin

During the first game, commentator GM Robert Hess commented: "I have so much respect for the way both these two handle the position. I learn a lot watching them play—their maneuvering is exceptional, it’s Karpovian!" In the game, however, the equilibrium was broken by one fatal move by Andreikin. Lazavik pounced:

A bishop sac that couldn't be accepted.

Andreikin wasn't disheartened, however, and came incredibly close to winning a rook endgame in game two.

That was drawn, as was game three, which was perhaps the wildest of the match. Andreikin suddenly broke through with a winning attack, but couldn't find the knockout blow, before at the end Lazavik took a draw by repetition in a position where he had a very easily missable but simple winning move.

Game 3 of the #SpeedChess Round of 16 match was wild, with first Andreikin, then Lazavik missing wins! https://t.co/Pljl2pUrI3 https://t.co/D9YmRLYxTH

— Chess.com News (@ChesscomNews) November 20, 2026

That set the tone for the match, as, following Lazavik's opening win, the remaining six 5+1 games were all drawn. Lazavik explained, "In general, when I don’t play well I just try to make draws and usually, if you don’t lose, you’ll win at some point, and that’s what happened."

3+1: Lazavik 5.5-1.5 Andreikin

The next win in fact came in the first 3+1 game, when Lazavik applied huge pressure with the black pieces until the white position fell apart.

Again, however, that didn't open the floodgates. The next two games were quiet draws, then in the third it was Andreikin who briefly had a chance to snatch a pawn with a winning position. Lazavik talked about the problem of not being able to exploit chances:

As I said in the interview before the tournament, it’s very important to see tactics well. It’s very hard to just outplay your opponent and take resignation, at some point he’ll try to do something, create some positional imbalance, and you need to calculate precisely a couple of moves or it’ll be very hard to collect points.

Lazavik talked to Aman Hambleton after the match was over.

11 games in, Lazavik was leading by just two points, but now he broke through and won the next four games in a row to all but clinch the match.

The first two games were 72 and 87 moves long, with Andreikin coming painfully close to saving both. In the third, the last of the three-minute section, Andreikin opened 1.h4!?. The surprising thing, perhaps, is that he got a decent position, but it then crumbled fast.

When Lazavik was asked if he'd noticed he'd gone unbeaten for so long in the match, he responded, "It’s much more important that he noticed it, and I think it affected him a lot, when he played 1.h4, he started tilting."

1+1: Lazavik 2.5-3.5 Andreikin

For a third segment in a row, Lazavik started with a win, this time in bullet chess, but finally Andreikin managed to hit back in the next game. It was suitably epic, with Andreikin ultimately weaving a mating net just when it seemed Lazavik might escape yet again. The game ended in 133 moves, with Andreikin smiling.

Andreikin smiles as he delivers checkmate on move 133 and finally grabs a win in game 16! https://t.co/hqxeH5ipRi #SpeedChess https://t.co/ah5G3VOXTq

— Chess.com News (@ChesscomNews) November 20, 2026

That cut the gap to five points, and Andreikin had excellent winning chances in the next game, but when he missed them the match was realistically over. Andreikin did grab one more win, but all he had was the consolation of winning the bullet section after a painful previous couple of hours.

Lazavik moves on to the Quarterfinals, where the players will already be competing for a spot in the Semifinals in London next year.

Lazavik will face the winner of So vs. Praggnanandhaa, and has a clear preference: "I think Wesley is a small favorite in general, so I would prefer to play against Pragg, and usually I do quite well against Indian players." Lazavik mentioned wins against GMs Arjun Erigaisi and Nihal Sarin.

Up next in the Speed Chess Championship, however, is Total Chess Pilot Champion Firouzja taking on Artemiev. Don't miss that match at 12:30 p.m. ET / 18:30 CET / 11 p.m. IST next Friday, November 27.

How to watch?

You can watch the event on Chess.com/TV. You can also enjoy the show on our Twitch and catch all our live broadcasts on YouTube.com/Chess. Games from the event can be viewed on our events page.

The live broadcast was hosted by GMs Aman Hambleton and Robert Hess.

The Speed Chess Championship, which starts on November 16 and culminates with Live Finals on February 7, 2027 in London, is Chess.com's most important speed chess event. Some of the biggest names in chess compete to determine the best speed chess player in the world. The games are played with time controls of 5+1, 3+1, and 1+1. The prize fund is $250,000.

title: Docuseries Featuring Gukesh, Other Top Indian GMs Begins November 22
summary:
A six-part documentary series titled Candidates: India's Chess Story will be releasing on YouTube, with the first episode airing on November 22. Viewership is free. The series follows the five Indian players at the 2024 Candidates Tournaments—GMs Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, Gukesh Dommaraju, Arjun Erigaisi, Vaishali Rameshbabu, and Vidit Gujrathi—exploring both the highs and lows of chess at their level, as India has grown into a chess powerhouse in the 2020s. Featuring on-screen contributions from Samay Raina and IM Sagar Shah, among others, Candidates was made by Dopamine Media in association with ChessBase India, MGD1, and Camera And Shorts. Chess.com assisted in marketing and other areas, and IM Danny Rensch was interviewed.

Candidates was created by Biswa Kalyan Rath and Prashant Raj, and filmed in nine different countries over more than two years. Dopamine has already released two short preview videos, a two-minute trailer on November 16 and a five-minute sneak peek on November 19. In addition to the five star GMs, Sagar, and Samay, IM Tania Sachdev and GM Peter Heine Nielsen (the longtime coach of GM Viswanathan Anand and then GM Magnus Carlsen) also appear.

Prashant Raj, who was also a director with Abhineet Chute, told the Times of India, "We started filming in 2022 without knowing how this story would end. We only knew these players were special and that someone needed to be in the room." Gukesh, of course, went on to win the 2024 Candidates and then the 2024 World Championship.

Now, ahead of the 2026 World Championship opening ceremony on November 22 and its first game on November 24, he is a key player in what is sure to be a compelling documentary. The official description from Dopamine begins: "In 2013, a seven-year-old boy sat in the stands in Chennai and watched Viswanathan Anand lose the world title. He vowed to win it back." Candidates shows the entire nation's path to Gukesh's eventual success in that vow.

The schedule for the series has been published, with all episodes premiering on YouTube at 7 p.m. IST/8:30 a.m. ET/14:30 CET (unless otherwise noted):

November 22

November 27

December 1

December 5

December 9

December 9 at 8 p.m. IST (immediately following Episode 5).

Chess documentaries have enjoyed a banner year in 2026: Queen of Chess in February, Untold: Chess Mates in April, Grandmasters in October, and now Candidates. They all tell a unique story about chess, demonstrating the depth of the game not only on the board, but in everything else surrounding it.
